lead: Any variable that changes the trapped air mass, the mixture strength or the timing moves brake power, brake thermal efficiency and emissions together. Engine ratings are quoted at agreed reference air conditions so that a result measured on a hot day or in a different test cell can be compared with the maker's figure. In a test cell, on a dynamometer and during certification, the observed result is corrected to the same reference conditions. Tuning a vehicle for altitude, humidity or fuel quality uses the same ideas. The aim is the shape of each curve, not just a list.
prereq: You need: 5.1 to 5.3 for the measured quantities; Unit 2 for ignition and injection timing; Unit 3 for knock.

sections.h3: Speed, load and the shape of BSFC

blocks.text: Speed changes three things at once: the trapped air mass per cycle, friction and pumping loss. Indicated power rises with speed until breathing becomes the limit, then falls. Friction power rises faster than indicated power at high speed. The gap between indicated and brake power therefore grows. Brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC) is fuel mass flow divided by brake power. BSFC has a minimum at mid-speed. At low speed, heat loss and friction are a large share of each cycle. At high speed, friction and pumping are large. Brake thermal efficiency is the reciprocal idea: η<sub>bth</sub> = 3600 / (BSFC × LCV) with BSFC in kg/kWh and LCV in kJ/kg, so the speed of minimum BSFC is also the speed of maximum brake thermal efficiency. The best efficiency is near the BSFC minimum. Load has a similar curve. At low load, friction and auxiliary losses dominate, so BSFC is high. It falls as load rises and is lowest around three-quarter load. At full load, SI engines enrich the mixture and CI engines reach the smoke limit, so BSFC rises again. The figure shows speed curves for correct and retarded timing.
BSFC = m<sub>f</sub> / P<sub>b</sub>;  η<sub>bth</sub> = P<sub>b</sub> / (m<sub>f</sub> × LCV)
blocks.where: m<sub>f</sub> is fuel mass flow in kg/s; P<sub>b</sub> is brake power in kW; LCV is lower calorific value in kJ/kg; η<sub>bth</sub> is brake thermal efficiency.

sections.h3: Mixture strength, equivalence ratio and timing

blocks.text: Mixture strength is best described by the equivalence ratio φ. It compares the actual fuel-air ratio with the stoichiometric fuel-air ratio: φ = (F/A)/(F/A)<sub>stoich</sub> = (A/F)<sub>stoich</sub>/(A/F). Here F/A is fuel-to-air mass ratio and A/F is air-to-fuel mass ratio. φ = 1 is stoichiometric, φ > 1 is rich and φ < 1 is lean. For SI engines, maximum brake power comes from a slightly rich mixture, with φ just above 1. The extra fuel improves flame speed and ensures that all air is used. Best brake thermal efficiency comes from a slightly lean mixture, φ around 0.85 to 0.95, because combustion is more complete, the throttle is more open (lower pumping loss) and no extra fuel is supplied beyond what the air can burn. Very rich mixtures raise CO and HC. Very lean mixtures slow combustion and can misfire. In CI engines the overall mixture is always lean; power is limited by smoke. Spark timing or injection timing sets where combustion occurs relative to top dead centre. Maximum brake torque (MBT) timing gives the highest brake torque at a given speed and mixture. Too much advance raises peak pressure, causes knock and raises NOx. Too much retard loses expansion work, raises exhaust temperature and can raise HC. The figure's retarded curve peaks earlier and lower. Timing and mixture together set CO, HC and NOx; see Unit 6 for the formation chemistry.

Intake air density sets the trapped air mass. Density is ρ = p/(R T), where p is absolute pressure in Pa, T is absolute temperature in K and R is the gas constant for air, about 287 J/(kg·K). A hot day or a high-altitude site lowers density, so brake power falls unless the engine is corrected or boosted. Humidity adds water vapour, which displaces some air and gives a small loss. The standard corrects measured power to reference air temperature, pressure and humidity. Observed power and corrected power are therefore different numbers. Always state which one you mean. Coolant and oil temperature matter. Cold coolant and cold oil raise friction and make fuel vaporisation poorer, so BSFC rises. Very hot coolant can cause knock and thin the oil. Carbon deposits raise the compression ratio, create hot spots and restrict breathing, so they can cause knock and raise NOx. Valve clearance that is too tight leaks compression and can burn valves; too loose reduces lift and makes noise. Exhaust back pressure raises pumping work, especially on a turbocharged engine, and reduces scavenging. Fuel quality matters. Octane number controls SI knock; cetane number controls CI ignition delay; calorific value sets energy per kg; density sets injected mass for a given volume. Compression ratio raises ideal efficiency but is limited by knock in SI engines and by peak pressure and NOx in diesels. Correction procedures are in 5.8.

figure.caption: Brake thermal efficiency against speed. Correct timing peaks near 2600 rpm; 10° retarded timing peaks earlier and lower.

spec.aria: Two curves of brake thermal efficiency against speed: the correctly timed engine peaks near 2600 rpm and higher, while a retarded engine peaks earlier and lower, staying below the correct-timing curve at every speed.

examples.question: A naturally aspirated diesel engine gives 40 kW brake power at 25 °C and 1.00 bar on a standard day. It is retested on a hot afternoon at 40 °C and 0.90 bar. Assume brake power follows intake air density. Find the density ratio, the observed brake power and the percentage drop.
steps: Convert the temperatures to kelvin: T_ref = 25 + 273 = 298 K and T_test = 40 + 273 = 313 K.
Use the density ratio: (p_test / p_ref) × (T_ref / T_test) = (0.90 / 1.00) × (298 / 313) = 0.8569.
Multiply by the reference brake power: P_obs = 40 × 0.8569 = 34.27 kW.
examples.answer: Density ratio = 0.857, observed brake power = 34.27 kW, a drop of 14.31 %.
examples.check:
p_ref = 1.00
p_test = 0.90
T_ref = 298.0
T_test = 313.0
P_ref = 40.0
ratio = (p_test / p_ref) * (T_ref / T_test)
P_obs = P_ref * ratio
drop = (P_ref - P_obs) / P_ref * 100.0
print(f'{ratio:.3f}')
print(f'{P_obs:.2f}')
print(f'{drop:.2f}')

traps: Quoting an observed power as the engine's rating. Test standards correct to reference temperature, pressure and humidity, so always state whether the figure is observed or corrected.
Reversing the equivalence ratio. φ > 1 is rich, not lean; φ < 1 is lean, not rich.
Thinking best efficiency and best power occur at the same air-fuel ratio. Best power is slightly rich; best efficiency is lean.
Retarding timing only to reduce NOx. Too much retard lowers efficiency, raises exhaust temperature and can raise HC and CO.
Blaming the engine when a hot day or high altitude lowers observed power. Intake air density has fallen; the engine may be unchanged.

quiz.a: φ = (F/A)/(F/A)stoich = (A/F)stoich/(A/F). φ = 1 is stoichiometric, φ > 1 is rich and φ < 1 is lean.

quiz.q: Why does BSFC have a minimum at part load rather than at full load?
quiz.a: At low load, friction and heat losses are a large share of each cycle, so BSFC is high. Around three-quarter load these losses are spread over more work, so BSFC is lowest. At full load, enrichment or the smoke limit raises fuel use again.

quiz.q: An engine gives 60 kW at 1.00 bar and 300 K. It is tested at 0.92 bar and 315 K. Assume power follows air density. Find the density ratio and observed power.
Using the figure, explain why the 10° retarded curve peaks earlier and lower than the MBT curve.
quiz.a: Retarded timing starts combustion late, so less heat is released near top dead centre and less work is obtained from expansion. Efficiency is lower at every speed. At high speed there is even less time for late combustion, so the retarded engine cannot hold its efficiency and peaks earlier.

quiz.q: Why is maximum power obtained slightly rich while maximum efficiency is obtained lean?
quiz.a: A slightly rich mixture improves flame speed and uses all the air, giving more power. A lean mixture burns more completely and needs less fuel for the same work, so efficiency is higher, but too lean slows combustion and can misfire.

quiz.q: Coolant temperature is kept too low. What happens to BSFC and why?
quiz.a: BSFC rises. Cold coolant and cold oil increase friction, and poor fuel vaporisation makes combustion less complete, so more fuel is needed for the same brake power.

quiz.q: On a hot, low-pressure day the observed power of a naturally aspirated engine is lower than its rated corrected power. Explain.
quiz.a: Hot air at low pressure has lower density, so each intake stroke traps less air mass. With less air, less fuel can be burned and brake power falls. The standard correction brings the observed result back to reference air conditions, so corrected power is higher than observed power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engine management systems continuously adjust fuel and spark or injection timing for air temperature, pressure and humidity, so the driver sees less of these effects than a fixed-calibration engine would show. Emission certification uses correction and driving cycles together, and real-driving tests add weather and traffic. Altitude kits for commercial vehicles and derating tables for generators are practical uses of density correction. Search next for SAE correction factors, engine derating, and altitude compensation in engine control units.
